title: Chapter 1: Early Years
primary_topics: Framing-prologue (89-year-old Artemio reflecting on his life) followed by Chapter 1: the birth and early childhood of Artemio V. Panganiban Jr. ('Dayunior') against the backdrop of the Commonwealth presidency of Manuel L. Quezon, the papacy of Pius XI, and the Great Depression -- with the Quezon administration shaped by the Catholic social encyclicals Rerum Novarum (Leo XIII, 1891) and Quadragesimo Anno (Pius XI, 1931), the same documents that would later define CJP's own life motto.

The Panganiban family origins as tenant farmers in Barrio Mandili, Candaba, Pampanga -- the eldest of eight surviving children Artemio Sr. ('Temi') marrying Patricia 'Agang' Villaseñor (daughter of the *cabeza del barrio* Igmidio 'Apong Midio'), the inherited cycle of *tiempo muerto* (fallow-period poverty), and the eloping move to Manila that began the family's slow rise.

World War II as the formative trauma of CJP's earliest years: the December 1941 evacuation from Manila to Barrio Mandili after Pearl Harbor and MacArthur's 'open city' declaration; the night-canoe journey separated from his mother for the first time, the *kapre* threats used to silence him, and the loss of voice on arrival; the Japanese raid that found the family photograph and saw Temi beaten in front of his children; and the gradual relocation to Candaba town via Mayor Servando Sagcal's offer of a secretary post.

Childhood survival as theological pre-history -- episodes that would later be reread as Providence: a six-year-old's dysentery cured without medicine through his mother's nursing alone; classroom Japanese under Imperial Army instructors; the 1945 American liberation bombs witnessed from under the Home Economics building; and his mother's Pampango plea to the soldiers that spared his father's life.

stances.claim: CJP's life is best read as Providential orchestration that became clear only in hindsight -- at 89, looking back, the 'confluence of events' that led to a relationship with God includes the humble birth, the lost parent, the newsboy years, and the sidewalks slept on. The Christian God he 'raged against' is read retrospectively as having been with him from his first breath.
stances.rhetorical_move: providential reframing of early hardship -- biography's organizing thesis stated in the prologue

stances.claim: The macro-environment of CJP's birth was already Catholic-social-teaching-shaped: Pope Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum and Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno animated Quezon's social-justice program, and the same encyclicals would later structure CJP's own life motto 'Liberty and Prosperity.' The world he was born into was already shaped by the documents he would one day live by.
stances.rhetorical_move: macro-framing of formation; doctrinal coincidence as biographical foreshadowing

stances.claim: Tenant-farmer poverty (*tiempo muerto*, debt-cycle, no medicine, no education) is not just background but inheritance -- the family's escape from Mandili to Manila and then back during the war defines the boundary conditions of CJP's whole arc. Coming from this base makes every later ascent legible.

WWII trauma -- the night-canoe separation from Ima, the *kapre* threats, the Japanese raid, the dog fights overhead at age 9 -- registered in the child before any theology could explain them. The 'lost voice' on arrival in Mandili and the recessive period after foreshadow a lifetime pattern of finding language through faith.
stances.rhetorical_move: psychological foreshadowing of later faith awakening

stances.claim: Two early near-death episodes -- the soldier's bayonet that spared Temi after Agang's Pampango plea, and the dysentery that should have killed a 6-year-old without medicine -- are presented as the first of many deliverances. The biography treats them as proto-evidence of the providential thesis ('only by understanding with faith did he appreciate...').
stances.rhetorical_move: providential deliverance pattern; cumulative evidence framing

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 opens with an 89-year-old Artemio V. Panganiban in his private museum at dusk, looking back on a remarkable career and concluding that 'Divinity had charted his course' -- the providential thesis that frames the whole biography. The chapter proper then situates his 1936 birth in Tondo against the Commonwealth presidency of Manuel L. Quezon, the papacy of Pius XI, the Great Depression, and the Catholic social encyclicals (Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum, Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno) that animated Quezon's social-justice program and would later define CJP's own 'Liberty and Prosperity' motto. His paternal line -- tenant farmers Wenceslao Panganiban and Honorata Pelayo in Barrio Mandili, Candaba, Pampanga, the eldest of their eight surviving children named Artemio Sr. ('Temi') -- had moved between Batangas and Pampanga in the agrarian *tiempo muerto* poverty cycle; his maternal line through *cabeza del barrio* Igmidio Villaseñor ('Apong Midio') produced Patricia 'Agang,' the Pampango-only-speaking homemaker who eloped to Manila with Temi. The Pacific War defines the chapter: after Pearl Harbor and MacArthur's 'open city' declaration, the family flees back to Mandili in a night canoe through San Miguel, Bulacan -- five-year-old Dayunior separated from his mother for the first time, terrorized by his aunts' *kapre* tales until his voice fails, arriving 'psychologically unresponsive' for days until reunited with Agang. A Japanese raid finds a framed photograph of a uniformed man and beats Temi as a suspected Hukbalahap supporter -- which he was, Luis Taruc being his friend -- until Agang's Pampango plea (which the soldiers could not understand but evidently felt) spares his life. The family then relocates to Candaba town when Mayor Servando Sagcal offers Temi a secretary post, lodging in the Home Economics Building of Candaba Elementary School where Dayunior begins first grade under Liling Sagcal and Imperial Army instructors. At six he survives dysentery with no medicine through Agang's continuous nursing -- a recovery 'regarded as a miracle' -- and in 1945 he watches the American liberation bombs from the underside of the Home Economics building. The chapter ends with the family at the 'threshold of a new chapter,' and with the prologue's claim quietly ratified: that everything that had already happened was 'an orchestration to realize a plan greater than he had envisioned for himself.'
